lesson_title: Fair or Free? The Economic Systems Seesaw
hook_text: Why do some countries have long bread queues and others have a whole aisle of bread?
clip_script: Two ways to buy bread. In a planned economy, the state decided last year how many loaves to bake and printed a cheap price on the wrapper. Everyone can afford it, but if the plan guessed wrong, the shop runs out by ten, and the price cannot rise, so people queue. One kind of bread. In a market economy, there is a whole aisle: white, brown, seed loaf, five brands competing for your money. Shelves stay full, bakers keep improving. But a family with no income still cannot buy. That is the seesaw. Freedom, choice and efficiency on one side. Equality and security on the other. Push one down and the other goes up. A mixed economy, like South Africa's, tries to balance it: a full aisle of choice, plus grants, schools and clinics paid for with taxes, plus a Competition Commission that fined bread companies for fixing prices. Balancing a seesaw is hard. That is why countries never stop arguing about it.
visual_style: Split screen of an empty shop with a queue and a full supermarket bread aisle, then an animated seesaw labelled freedom and fairness tipping as the systems change.
pacing: Two quick contrasting scenes, a slow seesaw reveal, a brisk South African landing.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and sort the statements into planned, market and mixed.
